entries.clue: At last Boris has a site suitable for a "short lie-down" (6)

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of Boris
suitable is read as made to suit, so the letters of a site are rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the five letters of A SITE rearranged

annotation.surface: Boris Johnson has found a nice spot for a quick nap.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads Boris as the prime minister scouting a place to doze; he only lends his final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short afternoon sleep, the lie-down of the clue.

entries.clue: Unorthodox source of Cold War souvenir, so the tourist is told? (3,3,4)

annotation.definition2: source of Cold War souvenir, so the tourist is told?

blocks.note: an idiom for eccentric or unconventional

blocks.clueFragment: source of Cold War souvenir, so the tourist is told?
blocks.note: read literally: chipped off the Berlin Wall

annotation.surface: A doubtful souvenir seller in Berlin assuring a tourist the chunk of concrete is genuine.
annotation.walkthrough: Fragments of the Berlin Wall, which split the city during the Cold War, are sold to visitors, who are told each piece came straight off the wall; the question mark hints they may not have.
annotation.definitionFit: Off the wall means bizarre or unconventional, so it matches unorthodox.

entries.clue: Dick, pissed, got red (6)

indicators.note: pissed means drunk, so the letters of got red stagger into a new order

annotation.surface: A man called Dick got drunk and went red in the face.
annotation.walkthrough: Dick looks like a man's name, the drinker who went red; it is slang for penis. Todger is British slang for the same thing.
annotation.definitionFit: Dick and todger are both slang words for the penis.

entries.clue: SNP's chief whip's 'hip' vocalising (4)

indicators.note: chief means head, so only the first letter of SNP is taken

blocks.note: the cat o' nine tails is a whip; the 's is read as is

annotation.surface: The Scottish National Party's chief whip singing about his hip.
annotation.walkthrough: The SNP is the Scottish National Party, and chief whip looks like a parliamentary job, but the phrase splits into S and a whip, the cat. Scat is the wordless jazz singing of hip musicians.
annotation.definitionFit: Scat is improvised jazz singing in nonsense syllables, a cool or hip way of vocalising.

entries.clue: Fat Greek ultimately involved with euro fiasco – panic! (5,3)

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of Greek is used
involved means tangled up, so the parts are mixed together
a fiasco is a shambles, so the letters are thrown into disorder

annotation.surface: A fat Greek caught up in the euro crisis, and everyone panicking.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the Greek debt crisis that shook the euro, with fiasco sounding like part of the story rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To freak out is to lose control in panic, so the two are interchangeable.

entries.clue: Brown-nose celebrity's butt? A bit weird (6)

indicators.note: a butt is a tail end, so the last letter of celebrity is used

blocks.note: a brown-nose is a toady, a creep

annotation.surface: Someone sucking up to a celebrity, perhaps getting a little too close to the star's backside.
annotation.walkthrough: Brown-nose conjures the literal image with the celebrity's butt; here butt only means the end of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Creepy describes something unsettlingly strange, a bit weird.

entries.clue: Shorts taken by defenders (6)

blocks.note: a defence lawyer takes on a case, called a brief

annotation.surface: Footballers at the back pulling on their shorts.
annotation.walkthrough: Defenders suggests a sports team in shorts; here they are defence barristers, who accept briefs, the instructions for a case.
annotation.definitionFit: Briefs are close-fitting short underpants, and a brief is a case handed to a barrister.

entries.clue: Fiasco means Labour frontbencher's finished (5-2)

blocks.note: Ed Balls, a senior Labour politician; the 's is read as is

annotation.surface: A political disaster spelling the end for a Labour shadow minister.
annotation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a Labour shadow chancellor who lost his seat in 2015. A balls-up is British slang for a botched job.
annotation.definitionFit: A balls-up is a mess or fiasco in British slang.

entries.clue: Webber's last score mangled by Brenda – "witch!" (8)

annotation.definitionNote: a witch is usually female and a sorcerer male, but both work magic

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of Webber
mangled means crushed out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

annotation.surface: The Queen savaging Andrew Lloyd Webber's latest musical score and branding someone a witch.
annotation.walkthrough: Webber's last score reads as his newest musical; it is only his final letter plus the word score. Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and she is ER.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: both words name a practitioner of black magic, though sorcerer usually suggests a man and witch a woman.

entries.clue: Acceptable to have an orgasm? Top bankers want theirs much-enhanced (6)

annotation.definitionNote: a description of the thing rather than a synonym
annotation.surface: A crude jibe that bankers' greed is a kind of sexual appetite.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole second sentence: what top bankers want boosted is their pay, their income.
annotation.definitionFit: Bankers are notorious for wanting ever bigger pay and bonuses, that is, income.

entries.clue: Be inclined to imbibe unknown amount being only half pissed? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Liszt is half of the rhyming slang Brahms and Liszt, meaning pissed

indicators.note: to imbibe is to drink in, so LIST takes Z inside it

blocks.note: a ship lists when it leans over
an algebraic unknown, like x or y

annotation.surface: A drinker who feels like having an unmeasured quantity but is only half drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: Brahms and Liszt is British rhyming slang for pissed (drunk), so Liszt alone is only half of it. The composer Franz Liszt is the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang Brahms and Liszt means pissed, so Liszt is literally half of pissed.

entries.clue: Arrange brief denial by Tony half doing a U-turn – one should get put away! (9)

indicators.note: brief means shortened, so negative is cut to NEG
half means only two of Tony's four letters are used
a U-turn goes back the way it came, so TO runs backwards

blocks.note: to put away food is to eat it

annotation.surface: Tony Blair's U-turn on a denial, and a cry that someone ought to be locked up.
annotation.walkthrough: Put away suggests prison, but here it means eating: food put away was ATE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of settling terms: you arrange a meeting or a loan by working it out with the other side.

entries.clue: (&13ac.) Ostentatiously wiggle your arse for our toy boy, as clued by Cyclops? (5,4)

blocks.note: booty is slang for the backside, so this is the phrase's plain meaning

blocks.clueFragment: for our toy boy, as clued by Cyclops?
blocks.note: a jokey tail: in slang booty also means a sexual conquest, the kind of toy boy a Cyclops clue would leer at

annotation.surface: An invitation to twerk for a young lover.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 12 and 13 across. Shake your booty, a disco phrase, means to dance by swinging your bottom about; the tail is Cyclops laughing at his own smutty clues.
annotation.definitionFit: Booty is slang for buttocks, so shaking it is wiggling your arse for show.

entries.clue: see 12ac. (5)
Labour's result, 1945-55 – Bobby Moore exchanged one for ring ... (4,6)

indicators.note: exchanged means swapped about, so the letters are both switched and rearranged
for means in place of, putting A where one O stood

blocks.note: a ring is round like the letter O

annotation.surface: A political verdict on the post-war Labour governments, bringing in the England captain Bobby Moore.
annotation.walkthrough: Labour looks political, since Labour governed from 1945; it means giving birth, and the post-war birth surge produced the baby boomers. Swap an O in Bobby Moore for A and rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Baby boomers are the children born in the post-war birth surge, the result of mothers' labour.

entries.clue: see 22dn. (7)
... "Labour can be given a leg-up by means of these": whip, uppity prick (8)

annotation.definition: Labour can be given a leg-up by means of these

indicators.note: uppity is read as going up, so in this down clue SPUR is written bottom to top

blocks.note: to whip cream is to stir it hard

annotation.surface: A continuation of 13 down, quoting a Labour boast about getting a boost, then insulting someone as an uppity prick.
annotation.walkthrough: The leading dots join this to the baby-boomer clue. Labour again means childbirth: a woman's legs are raised in stirrups on the delivery table.
annotation.definitionFit: Stirrups on a delivery bed hold a labouring woman's legs up, a literal leg-up.

entries.clue: Dotty met Boris knocking one out – criminal (7)

indicators.note: dotty means crazy, so the remaining letters are jumbled
knocking and out together mean removing, so the I leaves
completes knocking out, meaning to remove

annotation.surface: A dotty woman met Boris and punched someone out, a criminal act.
annotation.walkthrough: Dotty looks like a woman's name here, the one who met Boris; it tells you to scramble. Knocking out reads as a punch but removes the I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a member of an organised gang is a criminal by trade, the noun sense the clue ends on.

entries.clue: Merkel chiefly put in order? Rubbish! (6)

indicators.note: chiefly means at the head, so only the first letter of Merkel

annotation.surface: Angela Merkel lays down the law and someone shouts that it's nonsense.
annotation.walkthrough: Rubbish looks like a noun or an exclamation; as a British verb it means to disparage, which malign also means.
annotation.definitionFit: To rubbish someone is to criticise them harshly, to malign them.

entries.clue: Gnasher's balls: puts back in suspense (7)

indicators.note: to balls something up is to botch it, so the letters are mangled

blocks.note: taken letter for letter; the 's is read as is

annotation.surface: A report on the testicles of Gnasher, the dog, and whether they were put back.
annotation.walkthrough: Gnasher is the snarling dog in the British comic The Beano. Suspense means hanging, so something rehung is put back into suspension.
annotation.definitionFit: To rehang a picture is to hang it up again, putting it back in suspension.

entries.clue: Wanker ultimately into top sea food (5)

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of wanker
into means going inside, so R goes inside KILL

blocks.note: to top someone is slang for to kill them

annotation.surface: An insult, a sea and some food, strung into a vulgar headline.
annotation.walkthrough: Top is British slang for kill. Sea food is split: krill are tiny sea creatures that whales feed on, not seafood on a menu.
annotation.definitionFit: Krill are small shrimp-like creatures eaten in vast numbers by whales, food in the sea.

entries.clue: School's after equipment - cheap, vulgar stuff (6)

indicators.note: after means following, so SCH comes behind KIT

blocks.note: a standard abbreviation of school; the 's is read as is

annotation.surface: A school's sports kit dismissed as tacky tat.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads school first, but after places it second in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Kitsch is showy, tasteless art or ornament, cheap and vulgar.

entries.clue: Parrot Cherie, professionally: "Vote here" (4,5)

annotation.definitionNote: a place described by what you do there

indicators.note: professionally means under her working name, so Cherie Blair gives BOOTH

blocks.note: Poll is a traditional name for a parrot
Cherie Blair works as a barrister under her maiden name, Cherie Booth

annotation.surface: A parrot squawking an election slogan in Cherie Blair's direction.
annotation.walkthrough: Cherie Blair, wife of Tony Blair, practises law as Cherie Booth. Parrot suggests repeating, but it is Poll, the stock name for a pet parrot.
annotation.definitionFit: A poll booth is the booth where a voter marks the ballot.

entries.clue: Prince wants fabric hot bottom support (6)

blocks.note: lint is a soft linen fabric used for dressings

annotation.surface: A prince demanding hot fabric to support his backside.
annotation.walkthrough: Bottom support reads like underwear for a royal behind; a plinth is the base under a statue or column.
annotation.definitionFit: A plinth is the base on which a column or statue stands, support at the bottom.

entries.clue: Openly gay and keen to produce public disapproval (6)

blocks.note: to keen is to wail in grief

annotation.surface: Someone openly gay and eager, provoking a public backlash.
annotation.walkthrough: Keen reads as eager, but here it is the verb to keen, to wail.
annotation.definitionFit: An outcry is a loud public protest, an expression of disapproval.

entries.clue: Reverse of high tension knocking off on the beat (9)

indicators.note: reverse means turned back to front, so HT becomes TH

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, as on electricity pylons
to knock off is British slang for to steal

annotation.surface: Police on the beat relaxing, the opposite of stress, as they knock off work.
annotation.walkthrough: On the beat looks like police patrol, and knocking off like ending a shift; they mean pulsing and stealing.
annotation.definitionFit: Something throbbing pulses rhythmically, on the beat.

entries.clue: (& 14ac.) Arse support success takes a long time (4)

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
something that takes an age takes a long time

annotation.surface: A slow, hard-won success at supporting someone's backside.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 22 down and 14 across. Back passage is a coy euphemism for the rectum.
annotation.definitionFit: Back passage is a euphemism for the anus or rectum, so it stands for arse.

entries.clue: Repeatedly lose an erection, going without head (5)

indicators.note: without its head means the first letter is dropped, so SOFTEN loses S

annotation.surface: A man complaining that he repeatedly goes limp.
annotation.walkthrough: Repeatedly looks like part of the complaint; it is the definition, often.
annotation.definitionFit: Often means many times, repeatedly.

entries.clue: Impose limit on Athens' chief financial centre's size (8)

indicators.note: chief means head, so only the first letter of Athens

blocks.note: the City is London's financial district; the 's is read as is

annotation.surface: A demand to cap the size of Athens's banking sector during the Greek debt crisis.
annotation.walkthrough: The City of London is Britain's financial centre, usually just called the City.
annotation.definitionFit: Capacity is the amount something can hold, its size.

entries.clue: Rubbish Miliband turned Tory darling? Sod all lost! (6)

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so ED runs backwards
lost means removed, so the O leaves Boris

blocks.note: sod all is British slang for nothing, and nothing is O

annotation.surface: Ed Miliband defecting to the Tories and fawning over Boris, a move that loses everything.
annotation.walkthrough: Ed Miliband led Labour; turned looks like changing party, but it just reverses ED. Sod all is British slang for nothing, the letter O here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: scattered fragments and wreckage left lying about are rubbish in the noun sense.
